name: Palacio del Infantado
label: Palacio del Infantado
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de España' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de España' (way/553653023): middle (148 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Palacio del Infantado, Guadalajara'.
notes: Gothic-Mudéjar palace with a famous Isabelline façade of diamond-point stonework.

text.description:
The Palacio del Infantado is a 15th-century palace in Guadalajara, built in the Isabelline style and once the seat of the Dukes of the Infantado. Its main front is the reason to come. The limestone is cut into rows of diamond points, the main doorway sits off-centre, and a gallery of balconies runs along the top. Together they make a bold, repeating pattern that suits a phone camera well. From the square you can take in the whole facade in one frame, with no need to stitch anything together.

The palace has been protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural since 1914. It was damaged in the Spanish Civil War, and since 1973 it has housed the Museum of Guadalajara.

For the photo, stand in the square directly facing the front. Take one straight-on shot with the doorway roughly central in your frame, then a second where you step slightly to one side so the diamond points show their depth. Turn on gridlines so the vertical edges and the balcony line stay straight. Then move in and photograph the stonework alone: the diamonds on their own make a good close-up. Keep people in the foreground if you want a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: The palace is in Guadalajara, Spain, and faces the Plaza de España (known locally also as Plaza de los Caídos). Its main front looks west across the square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Plaza de España in Guadalajara. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade. If the square feels too tight to fit the top balconies in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the diamond-pointed stonework and the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de España (directly in front of the main facade, which faces west). A full frontal view of the diamond-pointed limestone facade, with the off-centre main doorway and the gallery of balconies along the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the balcony gallery up with a horizontal line, keeping your phone level so the facade does not lean. Place the doorway off the centre line, as it sits in real life, and let the diamond pattern fill the rest. Then take a second shot at 2x or more of the stonework alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the pale limestone looks washed out against the sky. Keep Live Photos on if you like, in case anyone walks through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is reportedly good, when the low western sun lights the stonework (per one blog).

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the square, but the palace houses the Museum of Guadalajara, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The Plaza de España is an open public square that can be visited without a ticket.
In late afternoon the low western sun lights the west-facing facade and lengthens the shadows from the diamond points (suggested by one blog only).

name: Pantheon of the Duchess of Sevillano
label: Panteón de la Duquesa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque de San Roque' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque de San Roque' (way/149485762): middle (475 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/655922867: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Panteón de la Duquesa de Sevillano' (35 m across).
notes: Neo-Byzantine funerary monument with a rich mosaic interior.

text.description: The Pantheon of the Duchess of Sevillano is a funerary building in an eclectic style. It was designed by Ricardo Velázquez Bosco for María Diega Desmaissières y Sevillano, Countess of Vega del Pozo, who was known locally as the Duchess of Sevillano. Permission was granted in June 1887 and work finished in 1916, the year she died. The plan is a Greek cross, the walls are Novelda stone, and the dome is covered in purple tiles. That dome is the main reason to bring your phone. The purple-tiled dome is the standout feature, seen across the park. The best-known view is of the entrance with the dome and roofs rising behind it, seen across the Parque de San Roque. There is no need to go inside for this photo. The pantheon stands within a school campus with its own walls, so you shoot from the public park or street side. Start and take a wide shot of the whole building with some park in front of it. Then step in or zoom for the dome and the stonework. Check the line of the roof before you press the shutter, because the building is symmetrical and looks best when the gridlines show it straight. The porch of the nearby Ermita de San Roque may offer another view; check it is still open and unobstructed before relying on it.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Guadalajara, Spain, next to the Parque de San Roque. The pantheon stands inside a school campus beside the park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head to the Parque de San Roque in Guadalajara. From there it is about 3 minutes on foot to the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot of the entrance and dome across the park. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for the tiled dome and stonework. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole building, and keep it level so the edges do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque de San Roque (entrance side, facing the pantheon's approach from the park). The pantheon's entrance and its glazed dome and roofs seen across the park, the view most sources associate with the building. The porch of the Ermita de San Roque is another possible vantage point; check it is still open and unobstructed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the entrance on the centre line, with the dome above it. Keep a strip of park in the foreground to give a sense of scale. If the hermitage porch turns out to be accessible, you could use the porch opening as a frame around the pantheon.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the purple dome keeps its colour against a bright sky. Live Photos are not needed here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No time is specified for this spot. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and dome than midday.

text.access_note: Photograph the exterior from the public park or street side, because the pantheon stands inside a school campus. Interior opening hours are seasonal, so check locally if you want to visit inside.

sources.title: Pantheon of the Duchess of Sevillano

name: Palace of Antonio de Mendoza
label: Palacio A. de Mendoza
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Teniente Figueroa' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Calle del Teniente Figueroa' (way/684740611): middle (69 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/850810560: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (111 m across).
notes: Renaissance palace in the old town.

text.description:
The Palace of Antonio de Mendoza is a palace in Guadalajara, and it has been protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural, Spain's heritage listing, since 1931. For a phone photo, the easiest and most rewarding view is from the street. The palace front, with its balcony, stands beside the Piedad church. A small open garden sits between the two, so you can see both buildings together. Guides describe this corner of Calle Teniente Figueroa as having high architectural value, and it is easy to see why. The stonework, the balcony and the church portal all sit close together in one frame.

The palace is still used as a working secondary school, IES Liceo Caracense. That means the Renaissance courtyard inside is not a public open-air spot, and you should not count on photographing it. Plan your picture around the street front and the garden instead. Stand opposite the garden entrance, keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the building lines stay straight. Leave a little space around the balcony so it does not feel cramped. If a car or passer-by spoils the first shot, wait a moment and try again.
text.geographic_location: The palace is in the city of Guadalajara, on Calle Teniente Figueroa. It stands next to the Piedad church, with a small garden between the two buildings.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make your way on foot or by local road transport from the centre of Guadalajara to Calle Teniente Figueroa. The palace is at number 6 (it may also appear as number 8, so check on the day). Once you are on the street, look for the small garden between the palace and the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the palace front, the garden and the church portal in one frame. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x if you want a closer shot of the balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Teniente Figueroa (opposite the garden entrance, on the street side of the palace front). The palace's street front and its balcony, framed beside the church portal across the small garden. The palace is to the south of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the palace front with the horizontal lines. Put the balcony on one of the third lines and let the garden fill the gap leading to the church portal. If you use ultra-wide, keep the phone level and do not tilt it upwards, or the walls will lean inwards. Take a second, tighter shot at 2x of the balcony alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the street is quiet and the light is soft and even, such as a bright but cloudy day or earlier in the day.

text.access_note: The street front can be photographed from the public road, but the palace is a working school and its courtyard is not an open public space, so check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.

name: Chapel of Luis de Lucena
label: Capilla de Luis Lucena
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Concatedral de Santa María' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Concatedral de Santa María' (way/168821951): middle (64 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Chapel of Luis de Lucena'.

text.description: The Chapel of Luis de Lucena, also known as the Capilla de las Urbinas, is a small chapel in Guadalajara, and it is the sort of building that rewards a slow look. The outside is brick, with cylindrical turrets at the corners, crenellations along the top and deep overhanging eaves. That mix of textures and shapes gives you plenty to work with, even on a short stop. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1914, which is Spain's formal heritage protection. It stands opposite the Concatedral de Santa María, so the two buildings can share one frame. There are two good ways to photograph it. For a closer view, walk along the sloping Cuesta de San Miguel, which leads to the chapel, and photograph the turrets, crenellations and eaves from there. Keep your lines straight by using your phone's gridlines, and tap on the brickwork so the exposure is set for the wall rather than the sky.
text.geographic_location: The chapel is in Guadalajara, opposite the Concatedral de Santa María. The Cuesta de San Miguel, a sloping street, leads to it.
text.directions_text: Head to the Concatedral de Santa María in central Guadalajara. From there the chapel is to the north-east, about 78 m away, or roughly 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from near the cathedral frontage to show the chapel and the church together. On the Cuesta de San Miguel, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you want the whole brick front. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the corner turrets and crenellations.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Concatedral de Santa María (in front of the cathedral, looking across to the chapel). The chapel seen across the street from the cathedral frontage, framing its brick walls against the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the chapel's walls with the vertical lines so the brick does not lean. Leave a little of the cathedral frontage in the frame to give context. For a closer alternative, take a second shot from the Cuesta de San Miguel, aiming at the turrets, crenellations and overhanging eaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. Hold the phone level to keep the vertical lines straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight suits brick best, as harsh midday sun can flatten the colour and make shadows under the eaves very dark.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street; if you want to see inside, check the official site before you go, as opening is limited.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft daylight flatters brick, while harsh midday sun can flatten colour and darken shadows under the eaves.
Tapping on the brickwork and lowering the exposure slider helps when the sky is bright.
The interior has limited opening hours, so visitors should check before going.

name: Church of San Ginés
label: Iglesia de San Ginés
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Santo Domingo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Santo Domingo' (way/150218563): middle (76 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/334583550: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia de San Ginés' (50 m across).
notes: Church in the southern old town.

text.description:
The Church of San Ginés is a working parish church in Guadalajara, and it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1931, Spain's heritage protection for important buildings. What catches the eye is the front of the church: a single, heavy stone facade with two large buttresses and towers topped by belfries. The main facade faces west. The solid, simple shapes make it an easy subject for a phone, because the whole building reads clearly at a glance.

The best view is from Plaza de Santo Domingo, the square the church stands on. From there you see the building at an angle rather than straight on, which still works well for the buttresses and towers. For the full west-facing front, walk round to the west side of the square, where the open space lets you step back far enough to fit the facade, buttresses and both belfry towers into one frame without tilting the phone upwards too much.

Then walk round to the west side of the square and take another for the full front. Move a few steps left or right so the towers sit symmetrically on either side of the frame. Switch on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the buttresses up with them, so the building does not seem to lean. If you have time, Plaza Pablo Iglesias can give a quieter angle on the church, though check the framing on the day.

It is a place of worship, so be discreet if people are coming and going, and wait for a gap rather than asking anyone to move.
text.geographic_location: The church is in Guadalajara, on Plaza de Santo Domingo, which is the open square it stands on. Plaza Pablo Iglesias is a nearby square.
text.directions_text: Head for Plaza de Santo Domingo in Guadalajara. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is to set the square as your destination. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the square is too crowded to step back, and keep the building centred to limit stretching at the edges. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for a close shot of a belfry.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Santo Domingo (across the plaza from the main west-facing facade, in front of the church). The full stone facade with its flanking buttresses and belfry-topped towers, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the buttresses with the vertical lines so the towers stand straight. Keep the phone level and hold it at chest height rather than tilting it up, which makes the towers lean inwards. For a quieter angle on the church, try Plaza Pablo Iglesias, though check the framing there on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky is bright but even, such as a light overcast day or a clear morning, as this tends to show the texture of the stone without harsh shadows. If you plan to go inside or very early or late, check the church's opening times first.

text.access_note: The square is open to the public, but the church is a working parish church and its opening hours may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bridge of Henares
label: Puente del Henares
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque del Río Henares' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Calle Río Henares' (roads).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Bridge of Henares (Guadalajara)'.
notes: Historic bridge over the Henares river.

text.description: The Bridge of Henares is a long, low stone bridge over the River Henares in Guadalajara. It was built in the 10th century and widened after the Reconquista, so the stonework carries several centuries of history. It is 117 metres long and has been a protected Bien de Interés Cultural since 1931. It photographs well because of its repeated arches. Seen from the riverbank, they line up along the water and make a strong, simple shape. The park path gives you the river, the arches and a bit of greenery in one frame, which suits a phone screen. The best view is lower down, not from the top of the path. Walk down from the park footpath toward the water and the arches rise in front of you instead of sitting far away. Start with the default lens (1x) and fit the whole span in if you can. Then move closer for a tighter shot of two or three arches with their reflections. If you want a different angle, the new bridge nearby, Nuevo puente del Henares, shows the old bridge side-on and gives a good sense of its full length. Take a few frames at each spot, and check the edges of the picture for bins, signs and passers-by before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the River Henares in Guadalajara, next to the riverside park, Parque del Río Henares, which is reached from the Parque Fluvial. The park is a walk from the town centre around Plaza de los Manantiales.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Guadalajara around Plaza de los Manantiales, walk toward the river and the Parque Fluvial. Follow the riverside footpath in Parque del Río Henares and go down toward the water on the left-hand side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge and river together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and want several arches in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tight shot of the arches from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque del Río Henares (left-hand side of the park's riverside footpath, going down toward the water). A closer, lower-angle view of the bridge's arches and the river, taken from the riverbank path.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the line of the arches along the lower or upper third, keeping the horizon straight. Stay low so the arches rise above you, and keep some water in the foreground. If the water is calm, try to catch the arches in the reflection. For a different view, the nearby new bridge, Nuevo puente del Henares, shows the old bridge side-on along its full length.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arches to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Take a Live Photo if there are ducks or people moving on the path, and pick the best frame afterwards. Keep the phone level, because wide shots near the water tilt easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon usually suits stone and water best. Check the light on the day, because the sun's position changes with the season.

text.access_note: The bridge is open to pedestrians and the riverside park is a public space, but check the official site before you go in case of local closures or works.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits stone and water best.
Calm water may give reflections of the arches.
Ultra-wide lenses used close to the water can tilt the horizon more easily.
The park is a public space where there may be passers-by and signs in the frame.
Walking time of about 7 minutes is calculated from 461 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute.

name: Church of Santiago el Mayor
label: Iglesia de Santiago
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Teniente Figueroa' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Calle del Teniente Figueroa' (way/684740611): middle (69 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/850810535: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia de Santiago' (40 m across).
notes: Historic church near the Plaza de Santo Domingo.

text.description: The Church of Santiago el Mayor is a 14th-century church in the old part of Guadalajara, and it has been protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural since 1946. From the street it is a modest building. The south façade is plain brick with a stone portal and a flight of steps down to the entrance. That plainness is what makes it a good phone photo: the warm brick and the simple doorway sit well in a narrow street, and the picture shows a modest, plain exterior. The calm exterior also hides a Gothic-Mudéjar interior, which gives your visit a nice story to go with the shot. The nave sits below street level, so the steps are part of the scene. Walking up from the Palacio del Infantado, the church comes into view on your left, which makes a natural little photo walk. Take one wide shot to show the façade in its street, then move closer for a second picture of the stone portal and the brick texture. The apse is the church's most photogenic side, but it is seen from the rectory courtyard, which is not public, so stick to the street view. If you want to go inside, check opening hours and any works on the building before visiting.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Guadalajara, a short walk up from the Palacio del Infantado. The church faces onto Calle Teniente Figueroa.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near enough to name, so start from the Palacio del Infantado. Walk up Calle Mayor and into Calle Teniente Figueroa, and the church comes into view on your left. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the façade and the narrow street in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Try 2x or the telephoto for the stone portal and the brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Teniente Figueroa (Opposite the church front, on the side reached by walking up from the Infantado via Calle Mayor, looking at the brick façade and central portal). The church's simple brick south façade and stone portal, framed by the narrow street, with the entrance stairs and the building's modest exterior that hides the Gothic-Mudéjar interior. The church is to the west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the portal up with a vertical grid line, so the walls do not lean. Keep the street on one side to give a sense of place, and include the entrance stairs to show how the church sits below street level. Then step closer or zoom in for a second shot of the portal against the brick.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the portal to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright sky is making the brick look dull. Hold the phone with both hands in a narrow street, as the light can be low.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, when the brick looks its warmest. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder than harsh midday sun, which can leave the narrow street half in shadow.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship, so respect any services and dress expectations, and check opening hours and any works on the building before visiting.
claims_not_in_sources: Brick looks warmest in soft morning or late-afternoon light.
Midday sun can leave a narrow street partly in shadow.
Light can be lower in a narrow street, so a steady two-handed hold helps.
The church may be used for services, and visitors may be expected to dress respectfully.

name: Convent of las Carmelitas de San José
label: Convento Carmelitas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Ingeniero Mariño' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5166198: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic convent in the old town.

text.description:
The Convent of las Carmelitas de San José is a Carmelite convent in Guadalajara, near the co-cathedral, and its street-facing church front is the part most worth a photo. The facade is built of brick and stone in the Baroque style. It has a central doorway, the founders' coats of arms on either side, and the Carmelite arms above the convent doorway. These details give you plenty to pick out, even if you only have a minute.

The convent was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1992.

The facade faces Calle Ingeniero Mariño, so the simplest shot is from the street directly in front of it. The approach to the entrance is on a slope, so take a moment to find level footing before you frame the picture. Start with a wide view that shows the whole front, then move closer for the coats of arms and the doorway. Keep the phone upright for the full height of the facade, and turn it sideways if you want to include the street. Look out for passing cars and people, and wait a few seconds for a clear moment. The interior may not be open when you visit, so treat the exterior as the main photo.
text.geographic_location: The convent stands on Calle Ingeniero Mariño in Guadalajara, near the co-cathedral.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from the co-cathedral in Guadalajara and look for Calle Ingeniero Mariño nearby. The facade is on the street itself, and the approach to the entrance is on a slope. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. If the street is narrow and you cannot fit it all in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the coats of arms and the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Calle Ingeniero Mariño, in front of the church facade, which faces the street. From here the photo shows the brick-and-stone Baroque front, with the central doorway, the founders' coats of arms on either side, and the Carmelite arms over the convent doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the facade up with them, so the building does not lean. Put the central doorway in the middle for a balanced shot. Then take a closer second picture of the coats of arms. If you use the ultra-wide (0.5x), keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and wait for passing traffic to clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, when the stone and brick detail is clear. Check the light on the day, as the street may be partly in shade.

text.access_note: Entry is listed as free, but the church may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Church of San Nicolás
label: Iglesia de San Nicolás
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza del Jardinillo' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza del Jardinillo' (way/553653013): middle (82 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/850829780: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia de San Nicolás' (62 m across).
notes: Central church close to the main square.

text.description:
The Church of San Nicolás is a brick-fronted church on the edge of the Plaza del Jardinillo in Guadalajara, Spain. Its main facade is brick, with a stone Baroque doorway set into it. That mix of warm brick and paler carved stone gives a phone camera something simple and clear to work with. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1981, which is Spain's formal heritage protection for important buildings.

The best exterior view is from across the square, where you can take in the whole front of the church. The Banco de España building stands beside it in the same view, so the square, the church and the bank all sit together in one frame. Stand back far enough to keep the doorway and the top of the facade in the picture without tilting your phone upwards, which keeps the vertical lines straighter.

The default lens (1x) suits most people here. If the square is busy or you want a tighter shot of the doorway, a 2x or 3x zoom lets you pick out the stonework without moving closer. Turn on gridlines to line up the edges of the facade. If you plan to go inside, check the opening hours before you go, as the church may be closed at times.
text.geographic_location: In Guadalajara, on the edge of the Plaza del Jardinillo, with the Banco de España building beside it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Plaza del Jardinillo in Guadalajara. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole facade with the square in front. Switch to 2x or 3x zoom for a close shot of the stone Baroque doorway. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can fit in the bank building too, but it stretches the edges, so keep the church in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Jardinillo (across the square from the church's brick main facade, with the Banco de España building in the same view). The church's brick front with its stone Baroque doorway, framed by the square and the Banco de España building beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the doorway in the centre and use the gridlines to keep the edges of the facade straight. Include a little of the square in the foreground so the church feels part of its setting. The Banco de España building can sit at one side of the frame to show where the church stands.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour and the sky doesn't wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is lighting the facade rather than leaving it in shade, and when the square is quieter so fewer people are in the frame.

text.access_note: The exterior is seen from a public square; if you want to go inside, check the opening hours before you go.

name: Guadalajara Co-cathedral
label: Co-cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Santa María' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Santa María' (way/553653017): middle (100 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/168821951: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Concatedral de Santa María' (65 m across).
notes: Co-cathedral of Santa María in the old town.

text.description:
The Co-cathedral of Santa María la Mayor is a brick church in Guadalajara, in Castile-La Mancha. It is built in the Mudéjar style, a blend of Christian and Islamic building traditions that you can read in the horseshoe-shaped arch over the main doorway. It is one of the seats of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Sigüenza-Guadalajara, and it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural, Spain's heritage listing, on 12 July 1941.

It photographs well because the main facade faces an open square. That gives you room to step back and fit the warm brick front, the arched doorway and the tower beside it into one frame, which is hard to do on a narrow street. Guides recommend the square as a good place for urban photos of the church.

For a phone, the square is the right place to be. Stand on Plaza de Santa María, face the facade and take your first shot with the default lens (1x). Then try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the tower gets cut off. Keep your phone upright so the tower stays tall in the picture, and switch on the gridlines so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. Tap the brickwork to set focus and lower the exposure slightly if the sky is bright. Before you go, check the official site for visiting arrangements, in case you want to see inside as well.
text.geographic_location: The Co-cathedral stands in Guadalajara, facing the Plaza de Santa María, with calle Doctor Santiago Ramón y Cajal running beside it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make your way to the Plaza de Santa María in Guadalajara. Walk towards the church and turn round to face the main facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and the tower together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole front and the open square, and a 2x zoom if you want a closer look at the horseshoe-arched doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Santa María (in front of the main facade, which faces the square). The brick Mudéjar facade with its horseshoe-arched main doorway and the tower rising beside it, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the doorway near the middle of the frame and let the tower rise on one side. Use the gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight, and include a little of the open square at the bottom so the building has space around it. For a detail shot, zoom in on the arch and the brick pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brickwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. Turn on the gridlines in your camera settings. Hold the phone level to stop the tower leaning.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the brick looks warm and the facade is evenly lit. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows, but check on the day which light reaches the facade.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but this is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements inside.

name: Tower of Álvar Fáñez
label: Torre de Álvar Fáñez
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio' (way/80774753): middle (254 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Tower of Álvar Fáñez'.
notes: Medieval tower remaining from the old city walls.

text.description:
The Tower of Álvar Fáñez is a pentagonal stone tower, up to 14 metres high, that once formed part of Guadalajara's medieval defences. It has two levels, and the arched openings to each floor are on different sides because the building sits on sloping ground. That slope is what makes it a good photo subject. From the park below, the tower rises above the garden terraces, with the Infantado palace area behind it.

The tower is named after Álvar Fáñez, a Leonese nobleman and military leader of the 11th century who served as a lieutenant of El Cid. It was also used as a chapel to the Christ of the Mass, known as the Cristo de la Feria. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1921 and fully refurbished in 2004. Today it holds an exhibition about the origins of the city's coat of arms and the legend of Álvar Fáñez.

For a phone photo, start in Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio and look up at the tower with the terraces in front. If you want the tower's front face and its large arched doorway straight on, walk round to Calle de Alvarfáñez de Minaya and shoot from street level instead. Keep the phone level so the stonework does not lean, and let the greenery in the park frame the shot.
text.geographic_location: In the old part of Guadalajara, standing above Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio, with the Infantado palace area beyond it.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Guadalajara, head on foot to Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio, which lies at the foot of the tower. The lower-floor entrance from the park is steep, so take care on the slope. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower and the garden terraces into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view of the stonework. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the arched openings and masonry.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio (lower park, below the tower's west side). The tower rising above the park's garden terraces, with the Infantado palace area in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the terraces filling the lower third. Tilt the phone up only slightly so the walls do not lean inwards too much. For a second view, try Calle de Alvarfáñez de Minaya, where you can photograph the front face and its large arched doorway straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters stonework, and the park is easiest to photograph when it is quiet.

text.access_note: The park and the street are open public spaces, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside the tower, as visiting rules may apply.
